title: soldier shot by police had pellet gun: source
article: A man shot to death by Winnipeg police this week spent two decades with the Canadian military, but was discharged in 2004 because of anger management issues, the Free Press has learned.
A family acquaintance also said a distraught Roy Thomas Bell, 44, confronted police with a type of pellet gun that closely resembles a real firearm.

Bell was shot and killed behind a Langside Street apartment block Monday night in an incident some residents described as "suicide by cop." Witnesses say Bell ignored repeated demands from two officers to drop the airsoft replica pistol and, at one point, dared officers to shoot him.
Police won't comment on whether the man forced officers into a situation where they had to shoot him.

Bell served more than 23 years in the 17 Wing post office at CFB Winnipeg, but was discharged three years ago when the military deemed he was unfit for active duty overseas, a family acquaintance said today.

The acquaintance said following the discharge, Bell had a dispute with the military and with Veterans Affairs over access to a psychiatrist. That care would have been funded by the military and Veterans Affairs.
But Bell was only approved for 12 visits each year with a psychologist, who was not authorized to presribe anti-psychotic medications, the acquaintance said.
Monday's deadly incident was the climax of that dispute.

According to the acquaintance, Bell armed himself with an airsoft replica gun - closely resembling a police Glock service handgun - and made his way to a friend's home Monday night. The friend had allegedly made an offhanded remark two days earlier - a remark that Bell took as a personal insult.
The family acquaintance said there was no way police could have known the gun wasn't real.

"Suicide by cop" is a term that refers to incidents in which a despondent person, knowing police are armed, puts himself into a position in which police have no option but to shoot. Police are trained to use lethal force to stop the threat against them and others, not to wound or shoot a weapon out of a person's hands.
Patrick Murdock, whose apartment also overlooks the area where the shooting took place, told CBC he also heard four shots.
"All I heard was some yelling," he said. "I heard somebody say, 'F-ing shoot me already!' and then I heard four shots, and everything was kind of quiet after that."
Brent Beckman, who lives at 34 Langside St., said he heard the shots at about 11 p.m.
"I was just about to leave for work when I heard the shots. It was so quick, like a machine gun," the Free Press employee said.

"I thought it was fireworks, but there were no gaps. I walked downstairs and just as I was about to grab the handle of the door I saw two people leaning over someone on the ground," he said. "I opened the door and one of the guys ordered me back inside. I wasn't going to argue.
"The guy was out. They tried to resuscitate him... they were pumping his chest."
Police were sent to the block after an unidentified tenant called 911 saying another man was threatening his safety, according to Sgt. Kelly Dennison, spokesman for the WPS.
"Our caller was obviously very afraid," Dennison said.
Bell and the other person knew one another, but Dennison said the incident was not a domestic call.

The first two-officer patrol car on the scene - two, two-officer units were dispatched - arrived within minutes. It's believed the officers knew from the original dispatch that they might be dealing with an armed individual.

Dennison said when the two officers walked around the building from the front street they came face to face with the suspect. He apparently had also just arrived - it's believed he never got into the building - after walking down the back lane between Furby Street.

In a relatively small area behind the block - an area not that much bigger than an average 12-foot-by-18-foot living room - the man then pointed a firearm at the two officers. He was also armed with a baseball bat.

It's believed one of the officers already had his handgun unholstered while his partner was armed with a Taser. In the next few seconds that officer fired the Taser at the man to immobilize him, but it didn't work.

A Taser fires two probes that both must connect to a person in order to emit a five-second, 50,000-volt burst. If one probe fails to hit, or if the target is too far away or winter clothing too thick, the Taser doesn't connect properly.
Police also said there have been instances where a Taser has had no effect on an extremely combative or drug-induced person.
Dennison said in this case it's not known why the Taser was not effective in stopping the man.
He said in the following moments the man still threatened the two officers with his gun. That's when the second officer shot him.
Dennison said the officer feared for his life and that of his partner - and he acted "appropriately."
"We have to take appropriate action," he said. "That's what you pay us for.
"Our officers did everything they could to avoid a lethal situation."
Dennison said he couldn't comment on the number of shots fired or how many times the man was hit. The man was rushed to hospital, but died soon after arrival.

As per police policy, the two officers have been placed on temporary administrative leave as the shooting is investigated by the homicide unit. The two officers have about two to five years of experience.
Detectives will determine the circumstances leading up to the shooting and whether it was justified. Officers are also investigating a number of independent witnesses.
By law, an inquest must also be held.
